title: Applied HPC with R
text:
Preface
The R programming language (R Core Team 2023) can be fantastic for most daily tasks. But as soon as you start dealing with more complicated problems, you may face the for-loop bottle-neck. If you ever encounter such a problem, this book is for you. Applied HPC with R is a collection of talks and lectures I have given about speeding up your R code using parallel computing and other resources such as C++. The contents have been primarily developed during my time at USC and UofU.1
The book was written using quarto and is hosted on GitHub, where you can access all the source code.

title: Profiling R code
text:
A proposed workflow
Code profiling is a fundamental tool for programmers. With profiling, it is possible to identify potential bottle necks in your code, as well as exessive memory usage. Some important things to consider when profiling your code:
Here is a proposed workflow for profiling and optimizing your code in general
Here is a formula to follow when doing code profiling/optimization:

title: Profiling R code
text:
Ask yourself these questions before you jump into profiling:




If you succeed, then ensure that the profiling is done in a finite time, this is, use a subset of the data to avoid having long waits. Running the profiler will add overhead computing time, so try to keep it short (e.g., 1 minute).
There may be many things that could be optimized, focus on what would deliver the highest impact. Could be a function that is only called once but takes a long time to execute, or a function that is called multiple times but is relatively fast.
Before making any changes, ensure that you have a backup of your original code, as well as a copy of the current profiling results. You should also ensure to save (if possible) the outcome of the code.
Re-run the profiler and compare performance. If no changes are observed, then go back to step 2. Ensure the new version of the code maintains the same functionality as the original (check the results).

title: Profiling R code
text:
Profiling code in R
In the R programming language, the most used profiling tool comes with the profvis package. The package provides a wrapper of the Rprof function, which is a built-in R function for profiling code. The profvis package makes it easier to visualize the profiling results in a web-based interface.
To use profvis, you first need to install it from CRAN:
install.packages("profvis")
Then, you can use it to profile your R code like this:
library(profvis)

profvis({
  # Your R code here
})
This will execute the code and generate a visualization of the profiling results in a new browser window. You can also save the output using the htmlwidgets package:
pv <- profvis({
  # Your R code here
})

htmlwidgets::saveWidget(pv, "profvis.html")
Once open, you will see two visualizations: the flamegraph and the data. The flamegraph is one of the most useful visualizations. It directly maps the time and memory used by each line of code

The data visualization shows the distribution of time spent in each function. Using a tree structure, which allows taking deep dives into the call stack.







Tip



When developing R packages, it is a good idea to pair your profvis::profvis call with devtools::load_all() to ensure that all source code is available to the profiler. Otherwise, the flamegraph won’t show your code (it will say “unavailable”).

title: Profiling R code
text:
Exercise: Identifying the bottle neck1

# Generate data
times <- 4e5
cols <- 150
data <- as.data.frame(x = matrix(rnorm(times * cols, mean = 5), ncol = cols))
data <- cbind(id = paste0("g", seq_len(times)), data)

pv <- profvis::profvis({
  data1 <- data   # Store in another variable for this run

  # Get column means
  means <- apply(data1[, names(data1) != "id"], 2, mean)

  # Subtract mean from each column
  for (i in seq_along(means)) {
    data1[, names(data1) != "id"][, i] <- data1[, names(data1) != "id"][, i] - means[i]
  }
})

htmlwidgets::saveWidget(pv, "profvis-slow-code.html")

# In interactive mode, we can directly view the profiling results
if (interactive())
  print(pv)



Can you identify where is the bottleneck in the code? What would you do to speed it up?

Caching calculations in a ShinyApp
Below is an example of a plotly figure that is pre-recorded for a shiny app. The idea is that, if the figure does not need to be reactive, you can always pre-compute the results and store them on a file, in this case, as an HTML file:
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(plotly)
 
# Like we did with the simulations, we have a default filename
fn <- "plotly.html"
 
# Notice I'm adding the www because, outside of the
# server call, this writes directly to the top level.
# Once reading, it will read from www.
if (!file.exists(file.path("www", fn))) {
 
  message("Creating the file...")
 
  # if it doesn't exist, then it creates it and saves it
  p <- plot_ly(x = 1:10, y = 1:10) %>% add_lines()
  htmlwidgets::saveWidget(
    p,
    file = "www/plotly.html",
    selfcontained = TRUE
    )
} else {
  message("The file already exists!")
}
 
 
# Define UI for app that draws a histogram ----
ui <- page_sidebar(
  # App title ----
  title = "Hello Shiny!",
  # Sidebar panel for inputs ----
  sidebar = sidebar(
    # Input: Slider for the number of bins ----
    sliderInput(
      inputId = "bins",
      label = "Number of bins:",
      min = 1,
      max = 50,
      value = 30
    )
  ),
  htmlOutput(outputId = "plotlyOutput")
)
 
server <- function(input, output) {
 
  output$plotlyOutput <- renderUI({
    tags$iframe(
      src = "plotly.html"
    )
  })
 
}
 
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

title: Writing efficient R code
text:
Avoiding unnecessary steps
Many times, we can find shortcuts to reduce the amount of data processing we need to do. A great example is in the linear regression function lm(). The lm() function will go beyond finding the coefficients in a linear model, it will also compute residuals, fitted values, and more. Instead, we can use the function lm.fit() which only computes the coefficients:

set.seed(331)
x <- rnorm(2e3)
y <- 2 + 3 * x + rnorm(2e3)

# Comparing
microbenchmark(
  lm = coef(lm(y ~ x)),
  lm_fit = coef(lm.fit(cbind(1, x), y)),
  times = 10,
  unit = "relative"
)

Unit: relative
   expr      min       lq     mean   median       uq      max neval
     lm 6.175799 6.185906 7.557382 6.208816 6.609496 16.89933    10
 lm_fit 1.000000 1.000000 1.000000 1.000000 1.000000  1.00000    10

title: Writing efficient R code
text:
Reducing copy operations
Like in any programming language, copy operations in R can be expensive. Beyond increasing the amount of memory used, copy operations require tme to allocate memory and then copy the data. Modern R minimizes these by using copy-on-modify. This means that R will not copy an object until it is modified. For example, the following code makes multiple copies of X, but it is until the last line that R actually makes a copy of X:

set.seed(331)
X <- runif(1e4)
Y <- X
Z <- X

# Checking the address of the objects
library(lobstr)
obj_addr(X)
## [1] "0x55e5553b03e0"
obj_addr(Y)
## [1] "0x55e5553b03e0"
obj_addr(Z)
## [1] "0x55e5553b03e0"

Modifying X will trigger a copy operation, and the addresses of Y and Z will remain the same, while X will have a new address:

# Modifying X
X[1] <- 100  # This is when R makes a copy of X
obj_addr(X)
## [1] "0x55e555748780"
obj_addr(Y)
## [1] "0x55e5553b03e0"
obj_addr(Z)
## [1] "0x55e5553b03e0"

title: Introduction to parallel computing
text:
Introduction
While most people see R as a slow programming language, it has powerful features that dramatically accelerate your code 1. Although R wasn’t necessarily built for speed, there are some tools and ways in which we can accelerate R. This chapter introduces what we will understand as High-performance computing in R.

title: Introduction to parallel computing
text:
Big Data
When we talk about big data, we refer to cases where your computer struggles to handle a dataset. A typical example of the latter is when the number of observations (rows) in your data frame is too many to fit a linear regression model. Instead of buying a bigger computer, there are many good solutions to solve memory-related problems:

Out-of-memory storage. The idea is simple, instead of using your RAM to load the data, use other methods to load the data. Two notewirthy alternatives are the bigmemory and implyr R packages. The bigmemory package provides methods for using “file-backed” matrices. On the other hand, implyr implements a wrapper to access Apache Impala, an SQL query engine for a cluster running Apache Hadoop.
Efficient algorithms for big data: To avoid running out of memory with your regression analysis, the R packages biglm and biglasso deliver highly-efficient alternatives to glm and glmnet, respectively. Now, if your data fits your RAM, but you still struggle with data wrangling, the data.table package is the solution.
Store it more efficiently: Finally, when it comes to linear algebra, the Matrix R package shines with its formal classes and methods for managing Sparse Matrices, i.e., big matrices whose entries are primarily zeros; for example, the dgCMatrix objects. Furthermore, Matrix comes shipped with R, which makes it even more appealing.

title: The parallel package
text:
Parallel workflow
Although R was not built for parallel computing, multiple ways of parallelizing your R code exist. One of these is the parallel package. This R package, shipped with base R, provides various functions to parallelize R code using embarrassingly parallel computing, i.e., a divide-and-conquer-type strategy. The basic idea is to start multiple R sessions (usually called child processes), connect the main session with those, and send them instructions. This section goes over a common workflow to work with R’s parallel.
(Usually) We do the following:
As we mention later, step 2 will depend on the type of cluster you are using. If you are using a Socket connection (PSOCK cluster), then the spawned R sessions will be completely, fresh (no data or R packages pre-loaded); whereas using a Fork connection (FORK cluster) will copy the current R session, including all objects and loaded packages.

title: The parallel package
text:
Create a PSOCK/FORK (or other) cluster using makePSOCKCluster/makeForkCluster (or makeCluster). How many child processes will depend on how many threads your computer has. A rule of thumb is to use parallel::detectCores() - 1 cores (so you leave one free for the rest of your computer).
Copy/prepare each R session (if you are using a PSOCK cluster):

Copy objects with clusterExport. This would be all the objects that you need in the child sessions.
Pass expressions with clusterEvalQ. This would include loading R packages and other code into the other sessions.
Set a seed (if you are doing something that involves randomness)

Do your call: parApply, parLapply, etc.
Stop the cluster with clusterStop

title: The parallel package
text:
Types of clusters: PSOCK

Can be created with makePSOCKCluster
Creates brand new R Sessions (so nothing is inherited from the master), e.g.
# This creates a cluster with 4 R sessions
cl <- makePSOCKCluster(4)
Child sessions are connected to the master session via Socket connections
Can be created outside the current computer, i.e., across multiple computers!

title: The parallel package
text:
Types of clusters: Fork

Fork Cluster makeForkCluster:
Uses OS Forking,
Copies the current R session locally (so everything is inherited from the master up to that point).
Data is only duplicated if altered (need to double check when this happens!)
Not available on Windows.

Other types are available via the function makeCluster from the snow R package (Simple Network of Workstations). These include MPI (Message Passing Interface) clusters and Slurm (Socket) clusters.

title: The parallel package
text:
A template program
The following code chunk shows a template for using the parallel package in R. You can copy this and comment the bits that you don’t need:
library(parallel)

# 1. CREATING A CLUSTER ----------------
nnodes <- 4L # Could be less or more!
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(nnodes)

# 2. PREPARING THE CLUSTER -------------

# Mostly if using PSOCK
clusterEvalQ(cl, {
  library(...) # Loading the necesary packages
  source(...) # Source additional scripts
})

# Always if you are doing random numbers
clusterSetRNGStream(cl, 123)

# 3. DO YOUR CALL ----------------------
ans <- parLapply(
  cl,
  ... long list to iterate ...,
  function(x) {
    ...
  },
  ... further arguments ...
  )

# 4. STOP THE CLUSTER
stopCluster(cl)
Generally, the ... long list to iterate ... will be a vector or another list that contains either data (e.g., individual datasets), a sequence of numbers (e.g., from 1 to 1000), a list of file paths (if you were processing files individually), or directly a short sequence with numbers from 1 to the number of nodes (least common application).
When calling parLapply or parSapply (the parallel versions of lapply and sapply respectively), the function call will automatically split the iterations across nodes using the splitIndices function. Here is an example of what happens under the hood:

# Distributing 9 iterations across two cores
(n_iterations <- parallel::splitIndices(nx = 9, ncl = 2))

[[1]]
[1] 1 2 3 4

[[2]]
[1] 5 6 7 8 9


Which means that the first R session will get 4 jobs, wereas the second R session will get 5 jobs. This way, each spawned R session (child session) gets to do a similiar number of iterations.

title: The parallel package
section: Example: Replacing a for-loop with parLapply
text:
Example: Replacing a for-loop with parLapply
One of the most common use cases for parallel computing is replacing a for-loop with a parallel version. In this example, we will call runif(10) 1,000 times, comparing a simple for-loop with parLapply.

Serial version using a for-loop
The serial version iterates over the simulations using a for-loop:

nsims <- 1000

# First, create seeds for individual runs
set.seed(1231)
seeds <- sample.int(1e7, nsims)

# Serial version using a for-loop
result_serial <- vector("list", nsims)
for (i in seq_len(nsims)) {
  set.seed(seeds[i])
  result_serial[[i]] <- runif(10)
}

# Looking at the first few results
head(result_serial, 2)

[[1]]
 [1] 0.38201608 0.30000010 0.03890397 0.51085385 0.63979380 0.26806211
 [7] 0.86383563 0.64311030 0.17286217 0.89551119

[[2]]
 [1] 0.23208922 0.65968122 0.55613334 0.75545780 0.25803644 0.89517280
 [7] 0.90952159 0.69711625 0.02608031 0.60768982


One thing to note here is that we are pre-generating a vector of seeds and setting the seed inside each simulation. While this is not a common practice for running things serially, as you will see, it is a common strategy for parallel computing that allows you to get the same results regardless of the number of cores/threads used.


Parallel version using parLapply
We can replace the for-loop with parLapply following the template we described earlier. Note the seeding strategy: instead of using clusterSetRNGStream, we are pre-generating a vector of seeds and setting the seed inside each simulation. This makes the results 100% reproducible regardless of the number of cores/threads used.

library(parallel)

# 1. CREATING A CLUSTER ----------------
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(4L)

# 2. PREPARING THE CLUSTER -------------
# We export the seeds vector to all workers
clusterExport(cl, "seeds")

# 3. DO YOUR CALL ----------------------
result_parallel <- parLapply(cl, seq_len(nsims), \(i) {
  # This makes it 100% reproducible, regardless of the
  # number of cores/threads we are using
  set.seed(seeds[i])
  runif(10)
})

# 4. STOP THE CLUSTER
stopCluster(cl)

# Results are identical
all.equal(result_serial, result_parallel)

[1] TRUE








NotePer-simulation seeding vs clusterSetRNGStream



The approach used here—generating seeds beforehand and calling set.seed() inside each simulation—is an alternative to clusterSetRNGStream. The key differences are:

clusterSetRNGStream initializes the L’Ecuyer-CMRG random number generator across the cluster. The streams depend on the number of workers, so results may change if you change the number of cores.
Per-simulation seeding (as shown here) assigns a unique seed to each iteration. Because the seed is tied to the simulation index rather than the worker, the results are identical no matter how many cores are used.

Both approaches are valid. Per-simulation seeding is especially useful when you want results that are invariant to the number of threads, for example, when debugging or comparing runs across different machines. Note that combining the two strategies is generally redundant: once you call set.seed() inside each iteration, the worker’s RNG stream initialized by clusterSetRNGStream no longer affects the draws in that iteration. Using clusterSetRNGStream alongside per-simulation seeding would only matter if you also rely on RNG outside the per-iteration set.seed() call, for example, in setup code running on the workers.

title: The parallel package
section: Example: Running a linear regression across multiple columns
text:
Example: Running a linear regression across multiple columns
In genomics, it is common to analyze genomic data at the gene level comparing expression levels against some phenotype/disease. A simple analysis consists of running a linear regression across multiple columns (genes) of a data frame. The following code-block generates some artificial data we can use for this example:

set.seed(331)
n_genes <- 10000
n_obs <- 1000

# A random matrix of omics
X_genes <- rnorm(n_obs * n_genes) |>
  matrix(nrow = n_obs)

# A random phenotype (completely unrelated for this example)
Y <- rnorm(n_obs) |> cbind()

We will wrap the analysis into a function so we can do benchmarking. We will use the lapply function to iterate over the columns of X_genes

ols_serial <- function(X, Y) {
  lapply(
    X = seq_len(n_genes),
    FUN = \(i) {lm.fit(X[, i, drop = FALSE], Y) |> coef()}
  ) |> do.call(what = rbind)
}

# Calling the function and looking at the first few rows
ols_serial(X_genes, Y) |> head()

               x1
[1,]  0.029403088
[2,]  0.008907854
[3,] -0.027246099
[4,] -0.031280262
[5,] -0.001309752
[6,]  0.066971469








Tip



Like we did in the efficient programming section, instead of using lm() or glm(), we can use lm.fit() for better performance. The lm.fit() function does less than the lm() function by skipping computing residuals and other overhead, making it faster for large datasets.


Using parallel computing (and following the template we presented earlier), this could be done in the following way with the parallel package:

library(parallel)

ols_parallel <- function(X, Y, ncores) {
  # 1. CREATING A CLUSTER ----------------
  cl <- makePSOCKcluster(ncores)
  
  # This will be called when exiting the function
  on.exit(stopCluster(cl)) 

  # 2. PREPARING THE CLUSTER -------------
  # We copy the data over
  clusterExport(cl, c("X", "Y"), envir = environment())

  # 3. DO YOUR CALL ----------------------
  parLapply(
    cl,
    seq_len(n_genes),
    function(i) {
      lm.fit(X[, i, drop = FALSE], Y) |> coef()
    }
  ) |> do.call(what = rbind)
}

# Checking it works
ols_parallel(X_genes, Y, ncores = 4L) |> head()

               x1
[1,]  0.029403088
[2,]  0.008907854
[3,] -0.027246099
[4,] -0.031280262
[5,] -0.001309752
[6,]  0.066971469








Tip



Just like the return(), on.exit() can only be used within a function call. We could have used stopCluster(cl) at the end as we do in our template example, but the benefit of using on.exit() is that it will be called automatically when the function exits, even if an error occurs. This helps to ensure that the cluster is always stopped properly.


Now that we have the function implemented, we can go ahead and (1) compare results and (2) measure performance.

library(microbenchmark)

microbenchmark(
  serial = ols_serial(X_genes, Y),
  parallel = ols_parallel(X_genes, Y, ncores = 4L),
  times = 10L,
  check = "identical"
)

Unit: milliseconds
     expr       min        lq      mean    median        uq       max neval
   serial  410.8463  413.8404  449.6835  453.7871  465.2267  509.7555    10
 parallel 1278.5510 1304.3986 1321.2432 1312.3034 1322.7910 1422.8523    10


From the comparison, we can see that the parallel version is significantly slower than the serial version. Two things to note here are (a) the task we are running is already fast (about 0.3 seconds on average for the serial run) and (b) there is an overhead cost associated with creating, preparing, and stopping the cluster. As we mentioned earlier, parallel optimizations only make sense if your code is already talking a significant amount of time, making the overhead cost associated with the setup relatively small. The following implementation of the function should make it significantly faster:

ols_parallel2 <- function(cl) {
  # 1. CREATING A CLUSTER ----------------
  # 2. PREPARING THE CLUSTER -------------
  # No need anymore as we are handling the core outside

  # 3. DO YOUR CALL ----------------------
  parLapply(
    cl,
    seq_len(n_genes),
    function(i) {
      lm.fit(X_genes[, i, drop = FALSE], Y) |> coef()
    }
  ) |> do.call(what = rbind)
}

# Checking it works
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(4)
clusterExport(cl, c("X_genes", "Y"))
ols_parallel2(cl) |> head()

               x1
[1,]  0.029403088
[2,]  0.008907854
[3,] -0.027246099
[4,] -0.031280262
[5,] -0.001309752
[6,]  0.066971469

# 4. STOP THE CLUSTER
stopCluster(cl)

The main differences from the previous version of the function are:

We are creating the cluster outside of the function and passing it as an argument.
We are exporting the X_genes and Y variables to the cluster only once, which should also reduce overhead significantly.
Because of the previous step, we are now calling X_genes directly in the main function.
The cluster is stopped outside of the function call (since the function no longer manages the cluster object).

Let’s measure the performance to see how much faster the parallel version is.

library(microbenchmark)

# We need to prepare the cluster before hand
cl <- makePSOCKcluster(4)
clusterExport(cl, c("X_genes", "Y"))

microbenchmark(
  serial = ols_serial(X_genes, Y),
  parallel = ols_parallel2(cl),
  times = 10L,
  check = "identical"
)

Unit: milliseconds

title: Slurm fundamentals
text:
What is Slurm
Nowadays, high-performance-computing (HPC) clusters are commonly available tools for either in or out of cloud settings. Slurm Work Manager (formerly Simple Linux Utility for Resource Manager) is a program written in C that is used to efficiently manage resources in HPC clusters. The slurmR R package–which we will be using in this book–provides tools for using R in HPC settings that work with Slurm. It provides wrappers and functions that allow the user to seamlessly integrate their analysis pipeline with HPC clusters, emphasizing on providing the user with a family of functions similar to those that the parallel R package provides.

title: Slurm fundamentals
text:
Definitions
First, some important discussion points within the context of Slurm+R that users, in general, will find useful. Most of the points have to do with options available for Slurm, and in particular, with the sbatch command with is used to submit batch jobs to Slurm. Users who have used Slurm in the past may wish to skip this and continue reading the following section.

Node A single computer in the HPC: A lot of times jobs will be submitted to a single node. The simplest way of using R+Slurm is submitting a single job and requesting multiple CPUs to use, for example, parallel::parLapply or parallel::mclapply. Usually, users do not need to request a specific number of nodes to be used as Slurm will allocate the resources as needed.
A common mistake of R users is to specify the number of nodes and expect that their script will be parallelized. This won’t happen unless the user explicitly writes a parallel computing script.
The relevant flag for sbatch is --nodes.
Partition A group of nodes in HPC. Generally large nodes may have multiple partitions, meaning that nodes may be grouped in various ways. For example, nodes belonging to a single group of users may be in a single partition, and nodes dedicated to working with large data may be in another partition. Usually, partitions are associated with account privileges, so users may need to specify which account are they using when telling Slurm what partition they plan to use.
The relevant flag for sbatch is --partition.
Account Accounts may be associated with partitions. Accounts can have privileges to use a partition or set of nodes. Often, users need to specify the account when submitting jobs to a particular partition.
The relevant flag for sbatch is --account.
Task A step within a job. A particular job can have multiple tasks. tasks may span multiple nodes, so if the user wants to submit a multicore job, this option may not be the right one.
The relevant flag for sbatch is --ntasks
CPU generally this refers to core or thread (which may be different in systems supporting multithreaded cores). Users may want to specify how many CPUs they want to use for a task. And this is the relevant option when using things like OpenMP or functions that allow creating cluster objects in R (e.g. makePSOCKcluster, makeForkCluster).
The relevant option in sbatch is --cpus-per-task. More information regarding CPUs in Slurm can be found here. Information regarding how Slurm counts CPUs/cores/threads can be found here.
Job Array Slurm supports job arrays. A job array is in simple terms a job that is repeated multiple times by Slurm, this is, replicates a single job as requested per the user. In the case of R, when using this option, a single R script is spanned in multiple jobs, so the user can take advantage of this and parallelize jobs across multiple nodes. Besides from the fact that jobs within a Job Array may be spanned across multiple nodes, each job in that array has a unique ID that is available to the user via environment variables, in particular SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID.
Within R, and hence the Rscript submitted to Slurm, users can access this environment variable with Sys.getenv("SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID"). Some of the functionalities of slurmR rely on Job Arrays.
More information on Job Arrays can be found here. The relevant option for this in sbatch is --array.

More information about Slurm can be found their official website here. A tutorial about how to use Slurm with R can be found here.

section: Step 1: Copy the Slurm script to HPC
text:
Step 1: Copy the Slurm script to HPC
We need to copy the following Slurm script to HPC (00-hello-world.slurm):
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --output=00-hello-world.out
module load R/4.2.2
Rscript -e "paste('Hello from node', Sys.getenv('SLURMD_NODENAME'))"
Which has four lines:

#!/bin/sh: The shebang (shewhat?)
#SBATCH --output=00-hello-world.out: An option to be passed to sbatch, in this case, the name of the output file to which stdout and stderr will go.
module load R/4.2.2: Uses Lmod to load the R module.
Rscript ...: A call to R to evaluate the expression paste(...). This will get the environment variable SLURMD_NODENAME (which sbatch creates) and print it on a message.

To do so, we will use Secure copy protocol (scp), which allows us to copy data to and fro computers. In this case, we should do something like the following
scp 00-hello-world.slurm [userid]@notchpeak.chpc.utah.edu:/path/to/a/place/you/can/access
In words, “Using the username [userid], connect to notchpeak.chpc.utah.edu, take the file 00-hello-world.slurm and copy it to /path/to/a/place/you/can/access. With the file now available in the cluster, we can submit this job using Slurm.

title: Slurm fundamentals
text:
Step 2: Logging to HPC

Log in using ssh. In the case of Windows users, download the Putty client.
To log in, you will need to use your organization ID. Usually, if your email is something like myemailuser@school.edu, your ID is myemailuser. Then:
ssh myemailuser@notchpeak.chpc.utah.edu

title: Slurm fundamentals
text:
Step 3: Submitting the job
Overall, there are two ways to use the compute nodes: interactively (salloc) and in batch mode (sbatch). In this case, since we have a Slurm script, we will use the latter.
To submit the job, we can type the following:
sbatch 00-hello-world.slurm
And that’s it! That said, it is often required to specify the account and partition the user will be submitting the job. For example, if you have the account my-account and partition my-partition associated with your user, you can incorporate that information as follows:
sbatch 00-hello-world.slurm --acount=my-account --partition=my-partition
In the case of interactive sessions, You can start one using the salloc command. For example, if you wanted to run R with 8 cores, using 16 Gigs of memory in total, you would need to do the following:
salloc -n1 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem-per-cpu=2G --time=01:00:00
Once your request is submitted, you will get access to a compute node. Within it, you can load the required modules and start R:
module load R/4.2.2
R
Interactive sessions are not recommended for long jobs. Instead, use this resource if you need to inspect some large dataset, debug your code, etc.




Yoo, Andy B., Morris A. Jette, and Mark Grondona. 2003. “SLURM: Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management.” In Job Scheduling Strategies for Parallel Processing, edited by Dror Feitelson, Larry Rudolph, and Uwe Schwiegelshohn, vol. 2862. Lecture Notes in Computer Science. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/10968987_3.

text:
How Slurm works
In the previous chapter we learned the vocabulary (nodes, partitions, tasks, CPUs) and submitted a “Hello world” with sbatch. Before we start running real analyses in the next chapter, it is worth spending a few minutes understanding what happens after you press enter. When something goes wrong on a cluster (a job that never starts, a job that dies without a message, results that never show up), the answer almost always lies in one of the moving parts we describe here.
This chapter has two parts:
No code needs to be run to follow this chapter. The only R output you will see comes from the package’s “verbose mode,” which prints what slurmR would do without submitting anything.

title: Under the hood: Slurm and slurmR
text:
The cast of characters
Slurm is a collection of programs that talk to each other over the network. Some of them run all the time (called daemons, the d at the end of slurmctld, slurmd, and slurmdbd), and others are the commands you type. Figure 6.1 shows how they relate to each other, and Table 6.1 describes each piece.






Figure 6.1: The main components of a Slurm cluster. Arrows indicate which component talks to which.






Table 6.1: Components of Slurm.










Piece
Where it runs
What it does




slurmctld
Management node
The “brain.” It keeps the list of all nodes and their state, holds the queue of jobs, decides which job runs where and when, and tells the nodes what to do. There can be a backup controller in case this one fails.


slurmd
Every compute node
The “worker.” It sits on a node waiting for instructions from slurmctld, starts the work, monitors it, reports back when it ends, and waits for more. It is often compared to a remote shell.


slurmdbd
Management node (optional)
Records accounting information (who ran what, for how long, using how much memory) in a database. This is where sacct gets its information.


Client commands
Login node (and compute nodes)
sbatch (submit a script), srun (run a command in an allocation), salloc (get an interactive allocation), squeue (list jobs), sinfo (list nodes and partitions), scontrol (inspect and modify), scancel (cancel), sacct (past jobs).






An important consequence of this design is that the login node is only a front door. When you type sbatch, the command does not run your script: it sends a request to slurmctld and returns. Your script will run later, on one or more compute nodes, under the supervision of slurmd.


Nodes, partitions, jobs, and job steps
In the previous chapter we defined nodes and partitions. Slurm adds two more concepts on top of them: the job and the job step.

A job is a resource allocation: “give me these nodes/CPUs/memory for this long.” Each job gets a unique job ID (the number sbatch prints after Submitted batch job).
A job step is a set of tasks launched inside a job, typically with srun. A job may have one step or many, running at the same time or one after another.

For example, one job may be allocated six nodes of a partition and run a single step that uses all of them, while another job splits its four nodes into two steps of two nodes each. Nodes that don’t belong to any job are free for other jobs to use.
For R users, the most common situation is simple: one batch script (the job) that calls Rscript once (so there is effectively one step). Whatever parallelism you want inside that job (multiple cores with mclapply(), a socket cluster, etc.) is up to your R code. Slurm reserves the resources, it does not parallelize your program.


The life of a job
Figure 6.2 follows a batch job from the moment you submit it to the moment it is recorded in the accounting database.






Figure 6.2: What happens when you run sbatch my-job.slurm.



In words:

Submission. sbatch reads your script, collects the #SBATCH options at the top (they are just comments for bash, but sbatch parses them), and sends everything to slurmctld. The controller checks that the request makes sense (does the partition exist? are you allowed to use that account? is the time limit allowed?), assigns a job ID, and puts the job in the queue. This is why sbatch returns immediately.
Waiting. The job stays PENDING until the scheduler finds a place for it (see How Slurm decides who runs where in the appendix of this chapter). The short version: ask for what you need, not much more (so the job fits in gaps and starts sooner) and not less (or Slurm kills it).
Allocation and launch. When the resources are available, slurmctld marks them as yours, and asks the slurmd of the first node of the allocation to run your batch script. Slurm sets a number of environment variables before doing so (SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURMD_NODENAME, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, …), and everything the script prints to the standard output or standard error goes to the file specified in --output (by default slurm-<jobid>.out in the directory where you ran sbatch).
Running. The script is a regular bash script: it runs commands one after another on that first node. If it calls srun, Slurm launches job steps on the allocated resources; if it just calls Rscript, a single R process starts on that node.
Completion. When the script ends, or when something forces it to stop, slurmd reports back, the resources are released, and the job’s final state and resource usage are recorded.

A job is always in one of a handful of states, which you see in the ST column of squeue and the State column of sacct. Figure 6.3 shows the most common ones, and Table 6.2 lists their codes.






Figure 6.3: Most common states of a Slurm job.






Table 6.2: Common job states.










State
squeue code
Meaning




PENDING
PD
Waiting for resources (or for a higher priority job to go first).


RUNNING
R
The job has an allocation and the script is running.


COMPLETING
CG
The script ended, and Slurm is cleaning up (some processes may still be active).


COMPLETED
CD
The script ended with exit code 0.


FAILED
F
The script ended with a non-zero exit code.


CANCELLED
CA
Someone (you or an admin) cancelled the job with scancel.


TIMEOUT
TO
The job reached the time limit (--time) and was killed.


OUT_OF_MEMORY
OOM
The job tried to use more memory than requested.






Notice that Slurm decides if a job succeeded based only on the exit code of the batch script. Slurm knows nothing about whether your R code did what you wanted; if R exits normally, the job is COMPLETED. We will see why this matters when we talk about error handling in slurmR.


Job arrays
Many problems in statistics and data science look like this: run the same program many times, changing only a small thing between runs. Simulating a model 1,000 times with different seeds, fitting the same model to 200 datasets, evaluating a grid of tuning parameters, or bootstrapping 5,000 replicates are all examples. Each run is independent of the others, so they can all run at the same time. These are known as embarrassingly parallel problems.
One way to handle this is to write a loop in R that goes over all the cases, and ask for many cores (what we did with mclapply() in the parallel chapter). This works, but all the cores must come from a single node, so you are limited to the size of the largest node, and Slurm has to find one big gap in the cluster big enough for the whole job. The other approach is to submit many small jobs, but typing sbatch a thousand times is clumsy, it floods the queue, and it makes the jobs harder to track.
A job array is Slurm’s answer: you submit one script with one sbatch command and tell Slurm to create N copies of it. Slurm treats each copy, called an array task, as an independent job: it has its own job ID, is scheduled independently (so one task may start right away on node 1, another a few minutes later on node 7, and a third one may wait until the evening), has its own allocation (the resources you requested apply per task, not to the array as a whole), and writes its own output file. The only difference between the copies is a number, the array index, which Slurm makes available to each copy in the environment variable SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID. It is up to your script to use that number to decide what to do: which seed to use, which row of a parameter table to evaluate, which chunk of the data to process, or which file to read.
Figure 6.4 shows a job array with four tasks.






Figure 6.4: A job array with four tasks. One submission creates four independent jobs that run the same script. They may start at different times, on different nodes, and finish in any order.



The size and the indices of the array are specified with the --array (or -a) option of sbatch:



Table 6.3: Examples of the --array option.









Option
Tasks created




--array=1-100
1, 2, …, 100


--array=1,3,5,7
1, 3, 5, and 7


--array=1-7:2
1, 3, 5, and 7 (a range with a step of 2)


--array=1-100%10
1, …, 100, but no more than 10 running at the same time






The last one is handy when each task reads a large file or hits a shared resource (like a database), and you don’t want 100 of them doing it at once.
Besides SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, Slurm sets other variables in each task, and offers file name patterns to keep outputs from overwriting each other:



Table 6.4: Environment variables and file name patterns of job arrays.





What
Variable
In --output use
Example in task 2 of job 36




ID of the array as a whole
SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID
%A
36


Index of this task
SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
%a
2


ID of this task as a regular job
SLURM_JOB_ID
%j
37


Number of tasks in the array
SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT

4






Slurm also lets you refer to a single task as <array job id>_<task index> (e.g., 36_2), which you can use with squeue, sacct, scontrol, and scancel. Cancelling 36_2 stops only that task; cancelling 36 stops them all.
From R, using the index looks like this. Suppose we want to evaluate a model over a grid of six parameter combinations, one per task. The R script (array-example.R) reads its own index and picks its row:
# Each array task gets a different value of SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
id <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID"))

# All tasks build the same grid, but each takes a different row
grid <- expand.grid(
  n   = c(100, 1000),
  rho = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
)
params <- grid[id, ]

set.seed(id) # A different seed per task
res <- my_simulation(n = params$n, rho = params$rho)

# Each task saves its own file
saveRDS(res, sprintf("result-%03d.rds", id))
and the bash script that submits it (six tasks, one core each) is
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=array-example
#SBATCH --output=array-example-%A-%a.out
#SBATCH --array=1-6
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
module load R/4.2.2
Rscript array-example.R
One sbatch array-example.slurm creates six jobs, each of which produces its own result-00X.rds and its own log array-example-<jobid>-<X>.out.
Job arrays also have a few advantages that make them the preferred tool for this kind of work:

Scale. The tasks can be spread over many nodes, so the limit is the cluster size (and the administrators’ limits), not the size of one node.
Faster scheduling. Smaller jobs fit more easily in the scheduler’s gaps (see backfill), and Slurm handles a whole array as a single submission instead of thousands.
Failures are contained. If task 17 runs out of memory, the other 99 are not affected, and you can rerun only the task that failed with, e.g., sbatch --array=17 analysis.slurm.
Easy bookkeeping. One job ID identifies the whole group, and each task’s output is in its own file.

Table 6.5 compares job arrays with the other ways of getting more than one CPU that we have seen so far.



Table 6.5: Three ways of using more than one CPU.










Strategy
Where does it run?
Who creates the parallelism?




Multicore job (--cpus-per-task=8)
One job, on one node, with 8 cores
Your R code (mclapply(), parLapply())


Multi-task job (--ntasks=8)
One job, possibly on several nodes
Your R code (e.g., a socket or MPI cluster)


Job array (--array=1-8)
8 independent jobs, anywhere in the cluster
Slurm; your script only uses the index






The slurmR package builds its Slurm_lapply() family of functions on top of job arrays, as we will see in the next part. For more details on job arrays, see the official documentation.

title: Under the hood: Slurm and slurmR
text:
How slurmR works

The idea
The slurmR package (Vega Yon and Marjoram 2019, 2022) is a lightweight wrapper around Slurm. Its design goal is to let you move from the parallel package to a cluster without learning to write Slurm scripts: just as parallel provides parLapply(), parSapply(), and clusterMap(), slurmR provides Slurm_lapply(), Slurm_sapply(), and Slurm_Map(). There is also Slurm_EvalQ(), which evaluates an expression in every job (like clusterEvalQ()), and makeSlurmCluster(), which creates a socket cluster out of a Slurm allocation (we use it in the next chapter).
The Slurm_*apply functions work like this: you hand over a list X and a function FUN; slurmR splits the list in njobs chunks, creates a job array with njobs tasks, and each task applies FUN to its chunk (using mclapply(), so each task can use several cores too). When all tasks are done, it puts the pieces back together. The result is the same as what lapply(X, FUN) would have returned, but the computation happened in as many different jobs as you wanted.
Everything is done by writing files. Every call to Slurm_lapply() creates, at least, two scripts: an R script with the work each array task has to do, and a bash script with the sbatch options that submits it. The data and the function are saved to disk (as .rds files) so that the tasks, which run on other computers, can read them. For this reason, the folder where slurmR writes must be visible from the compute nodes: a shared file system.


A job’s journey
In short, a call like Slurm_lapply(X, FUN, njobs = 2) goes through the following steps. In your R session, slurmR splits X in njobs chunks, saves the chunks, the function, and the options in the job folder, writes the two scripts (00-rscript.r and 01-bash.sh), and runs sbatch 01-bash.sh. Slurm then queues a job array (--array=1-njobs), and each array task runs Rscript 00-rscript.r: it reads its own chunk, computes, and saves its answer in 03-answer-<id>.rds. Meanwhile, your R session polls Slurm until all tasks have finished, Slurm_collect() reads and combines the answers, and, when you no longer need them, Slurm_clean() deletes the job folder.
The next sections go through each of these steps, using the package’s verbose mode to see exactly what is created. A timeline of the whole process is included in the appendix of this chapter.


Looking under the hood
The following example is from the package’s README (Vega Yon and Marjoram (2022)). We create 100 vectors of 50 random numbers each, and we want to compute the mean of each of them using Slurm_lapply():
library(slurmR)
#  Loading required package: parallel
#  slurmR default option for `tmp_path` (used to store auxiliar files) set to:
#    /home/user/project
#  You can change this and checkout other slurmR options using: ?opts_slurmR, or you could just type "opts_slurmR" on the terminal.

# Suppose that we have 100 vectors of length 50 ~ Unif(0,1)
set.seed(881)
x <- replicate(100, runif(50), simplify = FALSE)

ans <- Slurm_lapply(x, mean, plan = "none")

{

# The -snames- function creates the write names for I/O of files as a 
# function of the ARRAY_ID
snames    <- function (type, array_id = NULL, tmp_path = NULL, job_name = NULL) 
{
    if (length(array_id) && length(array_id) > 1) 
        return(sapply(array_id, snames, type = type, tmp_path = tmp_path, 
            job_name = job_name))
    type <- switch(type, r = "00-rscript.r", sh = "01-bash.sh",

}
TMP_PATH  <- "/home/user/project"
JOB_NAME  <- "slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18"

# The -tcq- function is a wrapper of tryCatch that on error tries to recover
# the message and saves the outcome so that slurmR can return OK.
tcq <- function (...) 
{
    ans <- tryCatch(..., error = function(e) e)
    if (inherits(ans, "error")) {
        ARRAY_ID. <- get("ARRAY_ID", envir = .GlobalEnv)
        msg <- paste0("[slurmR info] An error has ocurred while evualting the expression:\n[slurmR info]   ", 
            paste(deparse(match.call()[[2]]), collapse = "\n[slurmR info]   "), 
            "\n[slurmR info] in ", "ARRAY_ID # ", ARRAY_ID., 
            "\n[slurmR info] The error will be saved and quit R.\n")
        message(msg, immediate. = TRUE, call. = FALSE)
        ans <- list(res = ans, array_id = ARRAY_ID., job_name = get("JOB_NAME", 
            envir = .GlobalEnv), slurmr_msg = structure(msg, 
            class = "slurm_info"))
        saveRDS(list(ans), snames("rds", tmp_path = get("TMP_PATH", 
            envir = .GlobalEnv), job_name = get("JOB_NAME", envir = .GlobalEnv), 
            array_id = ARRAY_ID.))
        message("[slurmR info] job-status: failed.\n")
        q(save = "no")
    }
    invisible(ans)
}

The output has three parts: the R script (00-rscript.r), the bash script (01-bash.sh), and a final warning reminding us that the job has not been submitted and giving the command to submit it manually. The next sections explain each.






Tip



The call above did not submit anything but it did write files to disk, so you can inspect them. Once you are done looking, Slurm_clean(ans) removes them.




Where everything lives: the job folder
Each call creates its own folder, which slurmR calls the temporary path of the job. The name of the folder is controlled by two options:

tmp_path: the directory where job folders are created. By default it is the current working directory of your R session (the message you get when you load the package tells you the current value). You can change it for a single call with the tmp_path argument, or for the whole session with opts_slurmR$set_tmp_path().
job_name: the name of the folder (and of the Slurm job). By default it is a random name such as slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18, so two calls never collide.

The files of a job end up in <tmp_path>/<job_name>/. For the example above, using two jobs, the folder looks like this once the job has run:
slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18/
├── 00-rscript.r          # the R script each array task runs
├── 01-bash.sh            # the bash script submitted with sbatch
├── 02-output-<jobid>-1.out   # log of task 1  (created by Slurm)
├── 02-output-<jobid>-2.out   # log of task 2  (created by Slurm)
├── 03-answer-001.rds     # result of task 1  (created by the tasks)
├── 03-answer-002.rds     # result of task 2  (created by the tasks)
├── FUN.rds               # the function, shared by all tasks
├── INDICES.rds           # which elements of X went to which task
├── job.rds               # the slurm_job object (job ID, options, ...)
├── mc.cores.rds          # number of cores per task
├── seeds.rds             # one random seed per task
├── X_0001.rds            # chunk of X for task 1
└── X_0002.rds            # chunk of X for task 2
The files created before submission (00, 01, FUN, INDICES, job, mc.cores, seeds, and the X_* chunks) are written by your R session. The 02-output-* and 03-answer-* files appear only after the tasks run. Table 6.6 describes each of them.



Table 6.6: Files in the job folder.










File
Created by
Description




00-rscript.r
Your R session
The R script that every array task runs. The same script is used by all tasks; the tasks differ by the value of SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID.


01-bash.sh
Your R session
The bash script passed to sbatch, with the #SBATCH options. It calls Rscript 00-rscript.r.


X_0001.rds, X_0002.rds, …
Your R session
The list X split in njobs chunks, one file per task (by default parallel::splitIndices() makes consecutive, equally sized chunks). Each task reads only its own chunk.


INDICES.rds
Your R session
A list that records which elements of X went to each task, which allows putting the results in the right order.


FUN.rds
Your R session
The function to apply. Any other argument passed through ... or export is saved here too (as .rds files) and is shared by all tasks.


mc.cores.rds
Your R session
The number of cores each task uses with mclapply().


seeds.rds
Your R session
A vector of random seeds, one per task, so that tasks don’t generate the same random numbers (you can provide your own with the seeds argument).


job.rds
Your R session
The slurm_job object: the call, the options, the paths, and (after submission) the job ID. It is saved when the job is created and again after it is submitted.


02-output-<jobid>-<taskid>.out
Slurm
The log: everything the task printed to the standard output and standard error, including slurmR’s own messages ([slurmR info] ...) and any R error. One file per task.


03-answer-001.rds, 03-answer-002.rds, …
The array tasks
The results: the value returned by mclapply(X, FUN) for the chunk, one file per task.






Figure 6.5 shows who writes and who reads each file.






Figure 6.5: Who writes and who reads each file in the job folder. Blue: your R session. Orange: the cluster.









ImportantThe job folder must be visible from the compute nodes



The login node and the compute nodes must see the same files at the same path. Home directories and project or scratch spaces usually satisfy this, but local disks (like /tmp or a node-local scratch) do not: a file written to /tmp on the login node doesn’t exist on the node where the task runs, and the task will fail while reading its input. If in doubt, ask your system administrators which file system to use, and set tmp_path accordingly.








WarningReusing a job name erases the previous job



By default overwrite = TRUE, which means that if <tmp_path>/<job_name> already exists, slurmR deletes it and starts from scratch. This is not a problem with the default random names, but if you set job_name yourself, running the same call twice destroys the results of the first one. Use overwrite = FALSE if you want slurmR to stop instead.




The bash script
This is the bash script generated in the example (01-bash.sh):
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18
#SBATCH --output=/home/user/project/slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18/02-output-%A-%a.out
#SBATCH --array=1-2
#SBATCH --job-name=slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
/usr/lib/R/bin/Rscript  /home/user/project/slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18/00-rscript.r
It is a regular Slurm script like the ones in the previous chapters:

--job-name is the job’s name, slurmr-job- followed by random characters (it appears twice because it is added both by the function and by the options; the repetition is harmless).
--output sends the log to the job folder, using the patterns we saw in Table 6.4: %A becomes the ID of the array and %a the index of the task. This is how the 02-output-<jobid>-<taskid>.out files get their names.
--array=1-2 creates a job array with njobs tasks (the default is njobs = 2).
--cpus-per-task is taken from the mc.cores argument, and --ntasks=1 because each array task is a single R process.
The last line calls Rscript (from the same R installation as your current session) on the R script.

You can add anything else the script needs by using the arguments of Slurm_lapply():

sbatch_opt: a named list of options, each of them becomes an #SBATCH --name=value line.
preamble: commands to run before Rscript, such as module load. The preamble can be set for the whole session with opts_slurmR$set_preamble().
rscript_opt: options passed to Rscript.

For example, the call
job <- Slurm_lapply(
  x, mean,
  njobs      = 4,
  mc.cores   = 2,
  plan       = "none",
  job_name   = "my-means",
  sbatch_opt = list(
    account       = "my-account",
    partition     = "my-partition",
    time          = "01:00:00",
    `mem-per-cpu` = "2G"
  ),
  preamble   = "module load gcc/12.2.0"
)
generates the following bash script:
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=my-means
#SBATCH --output=/home/user/project/my-means/02-output-%A-%a.out
#SBATCH --array=1-4
#SBATCH --account=my-account
#SBATCH --partition=my-partition
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=2G
#SBATCH --job-name=my-means
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
module load gcc/12.2.0
/usr/lib/R/bin/Rscript  /home/user/project/my-means/00-rscript.r
Remember that, as we saw with job arrays, these resources are per task: the example above asks for four tasks with two CPUs each, one hour and 2 GB of memory per CPU each.






NoteDon’t use the preamble to load R



slurmR calls Rscript using the full path of the R installation of your current session (see the last line of the script), and it also copies your library paths (more on that below). Loading a different R with module load R/... in the preamble therefore has no effect on which R runs the tasks. Use the preamble for everything else the tasks need, such as a compiler or a system library (in the example, gcc); if you need another version of R, start your R session with that version.




The R script
The second file is the R script that every array task runs. It is long because slurmR writes it in a self-contained way (it does not even load slurmR: all the helper functions it needs are defined in the script itself). It can be read as five blocks:
1. Setup. The script sets the library paths to be the same as in your session, so the tasks find the same packages, and finds out which task it is by reading SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID:
.libPaths(c("/home/user/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/4.2", "/usr/local/lib/R/site-library", "/usr/lib/R/site-library", "/usr/lib/R/library"))
message("[slurmR info] Loading variables and functions... ", appendLF = FALSE)
Slurm_env <- function (x = "SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID")
{
    y <- Sys.getenv(x)
    if ((x == "SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID") && y == "") {
        return(1)
    }
    y
}
ARRAY_ID  <- as.integer(Slurm_env("SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID"))
If the script is run outside of Slurm (where the variable is empty) the ID defaults to 1, which allows testing the script by hand. It also defines snames(), a helper that builds the file names (00-rscript.r, 03-answer-%03i.rds, etc.) from the task ID, and stores the path and name of the job in TMP_PATH and JOB_NAME.
2. Error handling. Each step that could fail is wrapped in tcq() (short for “tryCatch quietly”). This is the function that deals with errors:
tcq <- function (...)
{
    ans <- tryCatch(..., error = function(e) e)
    if (inherits(ans, "error")) {
        ARRAY_ID. <- get("ARRAY_ID", envir = .GlobalEnv)
        msg <- paste0("[slurmR info] An error has ocurred while evualting the expression:\n[slurmR info]   ",
            paste(deparse(match.call()[[2]]), collapse = "\n[slurmR info]   "),
            "\n[slurmR info] in ", "ARRAY_ID # ", ARRAY_ID.,
            "\n[slurmR info] The error will be saved and quit R.\n")
        message(msg, immediate. = TRUE, call. = FALSE)
        ans <- list(res = ans, array_id = ARRAY_ID., job_name = get("JOB_NAME",
            envir = .GlobalEnv), slurmr_msg = structure(msg, class = "slurm_info"))
        saveRDS(list(ans), snames("rds", tmp_path = get("TMP_PATH", envir = .GlobalEnv),
            job_name = get("JOB_NAME", envir = .GlobalEnv), array_id = ARRAY_ID.))
        message("[slurmR info] job-status: failed.\n")
        q(save = "no")
    }
    invisible(ans)
}
If an error happens, tcq() prints a message to the log, saves the error in the task’s answer file (03-answer-<id>.rds) instead of the results, and quits R. Since q() exits with status 0, Slurm will consider the task as COMPLETED even though your function failed. The place to look for the problem is the log ([slurmR info] job-status: failed.).
3. Reading the inputs. Each task loads the objects it needs; notice that X_%04d.rds is formatted with ARRAY_ID, so each task reads only its own chunk:
tcq({
  INDICES <- readRDS("/home/user/project/slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18/INDICES.rds")
})
tcq({
  X <- readRDS(sprintf("/home/user/project/slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18/X_%04d.rds", ARRAY_ID))
})
tcq({
  FUN <- readRDS("/home/user/project/slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18/FUN.rds")
})
tcq({
  mc.cores <- readRDS("/home/user/project/slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18/mc.cores.rds")
})
tcq({
  seeds <- readRDS("/home/user/project/slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18/seeds.rds")
})
4. The computation. The task sets its seed (seeds[ARRAY_ID]) and applies the function to its chunk with parallel::mclapply():
set.seed(seeds[ARRAY_ID], kind = NULL, normal.kind = NULL)
tcq({
  ans <- parallel::mclapply(
    X                = X,
    FUN              = FUN,
    mc.cores         = mc.cores
)
})
5. Saving the answer. The result is saved in 03-answer-<id>.rds, and a final message is printed to the log:
saveRDS(ans, sprintf("/home/user/project/slurmr-job-113bd5bca5b18/03-answer-%03i.rds", ARRAY_ID), compress = TRUE)
message("[slurmR info] job-status: OK.\n")
Figure 6.6 summarizes what each array task does.






Figure 6.6: What each array task does when Slurm runs 00-rscript.r.





Submitting, monitoring, and logs
With the default plan = "collect", Slurm_lapply() writes the files, submits the job, waits for it, and collects the answers in a single call. slurmR submits the job by running sbatch and reading the job ID that Slurm prints (Submitted batch job 4242), then stores it in the slurm_job object (and in job.rds). After that it waits: it repeatedly asks Slurm for the state of the tasks (using sacct) until all of them have finished, either successfully or with a failure. How much of this happens in one call is controlled by the plan argument:



Table 6.7: The plan argument of Slurm_lapply() and friends.










plan
What Slurm_lapply() does
Returns




"none"
Writes the files only. Nothing is submitted.
The slurm_job object


"submit"
Writes the files and submits the job, then returns right away.
The slurm_job object


"wait"
Writes, submits, and waits until all tasks have finished.
The slurm_job object


"collect" (default)
Writes, submits, waits, and collects the answers.
The results (a list)












Note



With plan = "collect" or "wait" your R session is busy until the whole job ends, so if the session is closed (or you lose your connection to the cluster), you lose the connection to the job. The job itself keeps running, though. For long jobs, use plan = "submit", and come back later: read_slurm_job("<tmp_path>/<job_name>") reads the job.rds file and gives you back the slurm_job object in a new R session, and last_job() returns the last job submitted in the current session.


Once you have a slurm_job object (call it job), you can interact with it using the following functions, which are thin wrappers of the corresponding Slurm commands:



Table 6.8: Functions for working with a job.










Function
Equivalent to
What it does

sacct
A summary of the state of the tasks: 0 all done, 1 all pending, 2 all running, 3 some running, 99 some failed, -1 job not found (yet).

squeue
Pending and running tasks.

sacct
Information about finished (and unfinished) tasks.


Slurm_log(job, 1)

Shows the log of task 1.

Cancels the job.

sbatch
(Re)submits the job.






The logs (02-output-*.out) are where you should look first when something doesn’t work. (Slurm_log() shows them.) They contain anything your function printed with print() or message(), the [slurmR info] messages, R warnings and errors, and errors from Slurm itself (like exceeding the memory). A healthy task ends with:
[slurmR info] Loading variables and functions... done loading variables and functions.
[slurmR info] job-status: OK.


Collecting the results and cleaning up
When all tasks have finished, Slurm_collect(job) reads the 03-answer-001.rds, …, 03-answer-<njobs>.rds files, in order, and concatenates them into a single list. Since X was split in consecutive chunks, the concatenation puts the results in the same order as the elements of X, so Slurm_lapply(x, mean) returns what lapply(x, mean) would. Slurm_sapply() additionally simplifies the collected list (with simplify2array(), as sapply() does).
Slurm_collect() is picky: if any task is still pending or running, or if one has failed, it stops with the error Nothing to retrieve. Using any. = TRUE makes it read whatever answer files do exist, which is useful to take a look at partial results.
This is also where the job array design pays off. Suppose tasks 1, 2, and 15 to 20 of a 20-task job failed (say, they went over the time limit). You don’t need to run everything again, just those tasks:
# Submitting a simple job
job <- Slurm_EvalQ(slurmR::WhoAmI(), njobs = 20, plan = "submit")

# Checking the status of the job (we can simply print)
job
status(job)
sacct(job)

# Suppose some of the tasks are taking too long to complete (1, 2, and 15 through 20)
# we can stop them and resubmit only those as follows:
scancel(job)
sbatch(job, array = "1,2,15-20") # A new job ID will be assigned

# Once it's done, we can collect all the results at once
res <- Slurm_collect(job)

# And clean up if we don't need to use it again
Slurm_clean(job)
(This example was adapted from the package’s manual.) Because the inputs (X_*.rds, FUN.rds, …) are still in the job folder, sbatch(job, array = ...) just submits the same bash script again, restricted to the selected tasks.
The job folder is not removed automatically after collecting, so you can collect again later or look at the logs. When you don’t need it anymore, Slurm_clean(job) deletes the whole folder (it refuses to do so if tasks are still pending or running).






Tip



If you used plan = "collect", the function returned the results, not the job object. You can get the job back with last_job(), e.g., Slurm_clean(last_job()).




Other functions of the package
Two other functions of the package work differently, and we will see them in the next chapter:

makeSlurmCluster() submits a single job requesting several tasks, starts R worker processes on them, and connects to them from your session through sockets, like parallel::makePSOCKcluster(). This is not a job array.
sourceSlurm() lets you skip writing the bash script: you put the #SBATCH options at the top of an R script, and slurmR creates the bash file and submits it.

With this picture in mind, we are ready to run some code on the cluster.

section: How Slurm decides who runs where
text:
How Slurm decides who runs where
A cluster has many users and limited resources, so jobs usually have to wait. The scheduler (part of slurmctld) continuously looks at the queue and decides what to start next. The details are configured by each site, but the general idea has two ingredients:

Priority. Each pending job gets a priority number computed from several factors: how long it has been waiting (age), how much of the cluster you and your group have used recently (fair share: heavy users go back in the line for a while), the size of the job, the partition, and the quality of service (QOS) it was submitted under. Higher priority jobs are considered first.
Backfill. If the highest priority job needs resources that are not free yet (say, two whole nodes) the scheduler doesn’t leave the free resources idle. It looks for lower priority jobs that can run in the meantime without delaying the start of the higher priority job. To do so, it relies on the time limit each job declared with --time.

Figure 6.7 illustrates backfill in a two-node cluster. Job A is running on node 1 for four hours. Job B has the highest priority in the queue, but needs both nodes, so it must wait for A to finish. Node 2 is idle in the meantime, and job C (low priority, needs one node for three hours) fits in the gap and finishes before B is scheduled to begin, so it is started right away.






Figure 6.7: Backfill scheduling in a two-node cluster. Job C has lower priority than job B but is started first because it does not delay it.



This has two practical implications for you:

Ask for what you need, not for much more. Requests with shorter time limits, fewer CPUs, or less memory are easier to fit in the gaps, so they tend to start sooner.
…but not for less. If you ask for one hour and your job needs two, Slurm kills it at the one-hour mark (TIMEOUT). The same goes for memory (OUT_OF_MEMORY). Estimate your needs by running a small version of the job first (see the profiling chapter), and look at the report of finished jobs with sacct.

title: Simulating \pi with Slurm
text:
Submitting jobs to Slurm
The following is an example many people (including me) have used to illustrate parallel computing with R. The example is straightforward: we want to approximate pi by doing some Monte Carlo simulations.
We know that the area of a circle is A = \pi r^2, which is equivalent to \pi = A/r^2, so if we can approximate the Area of a circle, then we can approximate \pi. How do we do this?
Using Monte Carlo experiments, we can approximate the probability of a random point x falling within the unit circle using the following formula:
\hat p = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \mathbf{1}(x \in \mbox{Circle})
This approximation, \hat p, multiplied by the area of the square containing the circle, which has an area equal to (2\times r)^2, thus, we can finally write
\hat \pi = \hat p \times (2\times r)^2 / r^2 = 4 \hat p
We will primarily work by submitting jobs using the sbatch function. This function takes as its main argument a bash file with the program to execute. In the case of R, a regular bash file looks something like this:
This file has three components:
Submission is then made as follows:
The following examples have two files, a bash script and an R script, to be called by Slurm.

title: Simulating \pi with Slurm
text:
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=sapply
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00

module load R/4.2.2
Rscript --vanilla 01-sapply.R


The Slurm flags #SBATCH: These comment-like entries pass Slurm options to the job. In this example, we only specify the options job-name and time. Other common options would include account and partition.
Loading R module load R/4.2.2: Depending on your system’s configuration, you may or may not need to load modules or run bash scripts before being able to run R. In this example, we are loading R version 4.2.2 using LMod (see previous section).
Executing the R script: After specifying Slurm options and loading whatever needs to be loaded before executing R, we are using RScript to execute the program we wrote.


sbatch 01-sapply.slurm


Case 1: Single job, single core job
The most basic way is submitting a job using the sbatch command. In this case, you must have two files: (1) An R script and (2) a bash script. e.g.
The contents of the R script (01-sapply.R) are:
# Model parameters
nsims <- 1e3
n     <- 1e4

# Function to simulate pi
simpi <- function(i) {
  
  p <- matrix(runif(n*2, -1, 1), ncol = 2)
  mean(sqrt(rowSums(p^2)) <= 1) * 4
  
}

# Approximation
set.seed(12322)
ans <- sapply(1:nsims, simpi)

message("Pi: ", mean(ans))

saveRDS(ans, "01-sapply.rds")
The contents of the bashfile (01-sapply.slurm) are:
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=sapply
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00

module load R/4.2.2
Rscript --vanilla 01-sapply.R


Case 2: Single job, multicore job
Imagine that we would like to use more than one processor for this job, using the parallel::mclapply function from the parallel package.1 Then, besides adapting the code, we need to tell Slurm that we are using more than one core per task, as in the following example:
R script (02-mclapply.R):
# Model parameters
nsims  <- 1e3
n      <- 1e4
ncores <- 4L

# Function to simulate pi
simpi <- function(i) {
  
  p <- matrix(runif(n*2, -1, 1), ncol = 2)
  mean(sqrt(rowSums(p^2)) <= 1) * 4
  
}

# Approximation
set.seed(12322)
ans <- parallel::mclapply(1:nsims, simpi, mc.cores = ncores)
ans <- unlist(ans)

message("Pi: ", mean(ans))

saveRDS(ans, "02-mclpply.rds")
Bashfile (02-mclapply.slurm):
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=mclapply
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4

module load R/4.2.2
Rscript --vanilla 02-mclapply.R

title: Simulating \pi with Slurm
text:
Jobs with the slurmR package
The slurmR R package (Vega Yon and Marjoram 2019, 2022) is a lightweight wrapper of Slurm. The package’s primary functions are the *apply family–mainly through Slurm job arrays–and the makeSlurmCluster()–which is a wrapper of makePSOCKcluster.
This section will illustrate how to submit jobs using the makeSlurmCluster() function and Slurm_sapply. Furthermore, the last example demonstrates how we can skip writing Slurm scripts entirely using the sourceSlurm() function included in the package.

Case 3: Single job, multinode job
In this case, there is no simple way to submit a multinodal job to Slurm; unless you use the slurmR package.2 In this example, we will combine slurmR with the parallel package’s parSapply function to submit a multinodal job using the function makeSlurmCluster(). With it, slurmR will submit a job requesting njobs tasks (processors) that could span multiple nodes,3 and create a Socket cluster out of it (like using makePSOCKcluster.) One thing to keep in mind is that Socket clusters are limited in the number of connections a single R session can span. You can read more about it here and here.
R script (03-parsapply-slurmr.R):
# Model parameters
nsims  <- 1e3
n      <- 1e4
ncores <- 4L

# Function to simulate pi
simpi <- function(i) {
  
  p <- matrix(runif(n*2, -1, 1), ncol = 2)
  mean(sqrt(rowSums(p^2)) <= 1) * 4
  
}

# Setting up slurmR
library(slurmR) # This also loads the parallel package

# Making the cluster, and exporting the variables
cl <- makeSlurmCluster(ncores)

# Approximation
clusterExport(cl, c("n", "simpi"))
ans <- parSapply(cl, 1:nsims, simpi)

# Closing connection
stopCluster(cl)

message("Pi: ", mean(ans))

saveRDS(ans, "03-parsapply-slurmr.rds")
Bashfile (03-parsapply-slurmr.slurm):
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=parsapply
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00

module load R/4.2.2
Rscript --vanilla 03-parsapply-slurmr.R


Case 4: Multi job, single/multi-core
Another way to submit jobs is using job arrays. A job array is a job repeated njobs times with the same configuration. The main difference between replicates is what you do with the SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID environment variable. This variable is defined within each replicate and can be used to make the “subjob” depending on that.
Here is a quick example using R
ID <- Sys.getenv("SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID")
if (ID == 1) {
  ...[do this]...
} else if (ID == 2) {
  ...[do that]...
}
The slurmR R package makes submitting job arrays easy. Again, with the simulation of pi, we can do it in the following way:
R script (04-slurm_sapply.R):
# Model parameters
nsims  <- 1e3
n      <- 1e4
# ncores <- 4L
njobs  <- 4L

# Function to simulate pi
simpi <- function(i, n.) {
  
  p <- matrix(runif(n.*2, -1, 1), ncol = 2)
  mean(sqrt(rowSums(p^2)) <= 1) * 4
  
}

# Setting up slurmR
library(slurmR) # This also loads the parallel package

# Approximation
ans <- Slurm_sapply(
  1:nsims, simpi,
  n.       = n,
  njobs    = njobs,
  plan     = "collect",
  tmp_path = "/scratch/vegayon" # This is where all temp files will be exported
  )

message("Pi: ", mean(ans))

saveRDS(ans, "04-slurm_sapply.rds")
Bashfile (04-slurm_sapply.slurm):
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=slurm_sapply
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00

module load R/4.2.2
Rscript --vanilla 04-slurm_sapply.R
One of the main benefits of using this approach instead of the makeSlurmCluster function (and thus, working with a SOCK cluster) are:

The number of jobs is not limited here (only by the admin, but not by R).
If a job fails, then we can re-run it using sbatch once again (see example here).
You can check the individual logs of each process using the function Slurm_lob().
You can submit the job and quit the R session without waiting for it to finalize. You can always read back the job using the function read_slurm_job([path-to-the-temp])



Case 5: Skipping the .slurm file
The slurmR package has a function named sourceSlurm that can be used to avoid creating the .slurm file. The user can add the SBATCH options to the top of the R script (including the #!/bin/sh line) and submit the job from within R as follows:
R script (05-sapply.R):
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=sapply-sourceSlurm
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00

# Model parameters
nsims <- 1e3
n     <- 1e4

# Function to simulate pi
simpi <- function(i) {
  
  p <- matrix(runif(n*2, -1, 1), ncol = 2)
  mean(sqrt(rowSums(p^2)) <= 1) * 4
  
}

# Approximation
set.seed(12322)
ans <- sapply(1:nsims, simpi)

message("Pi: ", mean(ans))

saveRDS(ans, "05-sapply.rds")
From the R console (is OK if you are in the Head node)
slurmR::sourceSlurm("05-sapply.R")
And voilá! A temporary bash file will be generated to submit the R script to the queue. The following video shows a possible output on the University of Utah’s CHPC with slurmR version 0.5-3:

RcppArmadillo and OpenMP

Friendlier than RcppParallel… at least for ‘I-use-Rcpp-but-don’t-actually-know-much-about-C++’ users (like myself!).
Must run only ‘Thread-safe’ calls, so calling R within parallel blocks can cause problems (almost all the time).
Use arma objects, e.g. arma::mat, arma::vec, etc. Or, if you are used to them std::vector objects as these are thread-safe.
Pseudo Random Number Generation is not very straightforward… But C++11 has a nice set of functions that can be used together with OpenMP
Need to think about how processors work, cache memory, etc. Otherwise, you could get into trouble… if your code is slower when run in parallel, then you probably are facing false sharing
If R crashes… try running R with a debugger (see Section 4.3 in Writing R extensions):
~$ R --debugger=valgrind


RcppArmadillo and OpenMP workflow

Tell Rcpp that you need to include that in the compiler:
#include <omp.h>
// [[Rcpp::plugins(openmp)]]
Within your function, set the number of cores, e.g
// Setting the cores
omp_set_num_threads(cores);
Tell the compiler that you’ll be running a block in parallel with OpenMP
#pragma omp [directives] [options]
{
  ...your neat parallel code...
}
You’ll need to specify how OMP should handle the data:

shared: Default, all threads access the same copy.
private: Each thread has its own copy, uninitialized.
firstprivate Each thread has its own copy, initialized.
lastprivate Each thread has its own copy. The last value used is returned.

Setting default(none) is a good practice.
Compile!



Ex 5: RcppArmadillo + OpenMP
Our own version of the dist function… but in parallel!

#include <omp.h>
#include <RcppArmadillo.h>
// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppArmadillo)]]
// [[Rcpp::plugins(openmp)]]
using namespace Rcpp;
// [[Rcpp::export]]
arma::mat dist_par(const arma::mat & X, int cores = 1) {
  
  // Some constants
  int N = (int) X.n_rows;
  int K = (int) X.n_cols;
  
  // Output
  arma::mat D(N,N);
  D.zeros(); // Filling with zeros
  
  // Setting the cores
  omp_set_num_threads(cores);
  
#pragma omp parallel for shared(D, N, K, X) default(none)
  for (int i=0; i<N; ++i)
    for (int j=0; j<i; ++j) {
      for (int k=0; k<K; k++) 
        D.at(i,j) += pow(X.at(i,k) - X.at(j,k), 2.0);
      
      // Computing square root
      D.at(i,j) = sqrt(D.at(i,j));
      D.at(j,i) = D.at(i,j);
    }
      
  
  // My nice distance matrix
  return D;
}

Ex 6: The future

future is an R package that was designed “to provide a very simple and uniform way of evaluating R expressions asynchronously using various resources available to the user.”
future class objects are either resolved or unresolved.
If queried, Resolved values are return immediately, and Unresolved values will block the process (i.e. wait) until it is resolved.
Futures can be parallel/serial, in a single (local or remote) computer, or a cluster of them.

Let’s see a brief example

library(future)
plan(multicore)
# We are creating a global variable
a <- 2
# Creating the futures has only the overhead (setup) time

  x1 %<-% {Sys.sleep(3);a^2}
  x2 %<-% {Sys.sleep(3);a^3}
})

Bonus track 1: Simulating \pi

We know that \pi = \frac{A}{r^2}. We approximate it by randomly adding points x to a square of size 2 centered at the origin.
So, we approximate \pi as \Pr\{\|x\| \leq 1\}\times 2^2










The R code to do this

pisim <- function(i, nsim) {  # Notice we don't use the -i-

  ans  <- matrix(runif(nsim*2), ncol=2)
  
  # Distance to the origin
  ans  <- sqrt(rowSums(ans^2))
  
  # Estimated pi
  (sum(ans <= 1)*4)/nsim
}

Using GDB
Sometimes, we need to go further and inspect what’s going on inside the program. GBD is excellent for that. With GBD, we can set breakpoints that allow us to review the program while it is executed.
The following Rcpp code generates a memory not mapped type error:

// [[Rcpp::export]]
NumericVector faulty_program(int n) {

    return *x_ptr;

To inspect an error with GDB, we have to follow these steps:

Run R with gdb as debugger: R --debugger=gdb. R won’t start immediately, so we have time to add breakpoints.





We can set a breakpoint on the given function with break faulty_program. GDB will grab it on the fly, so choose yes. It most likely will warn you that there’s no symbol for that function.





Run R using the run command in gdb:





Source the program using Rcpp::sourceCpp, and wait for gdb to pause the program once it reaches the breakpoint.





Once the program has paused, we can inspect the context.





Because of the number of options it has, using GBD can be overwhelming. Here is the list of commands I use the most:

continue    # Continue running the program
next        # Execute the next step
bt          # Show the entire call stack (backtrace)
up          # Go up one level in the call stack
down        # Go down one level in the call stack
print       # Print/display an expression
